intro: Two arts in this unit meet in a shape. Capoeira is played in a roda, a circle of people with music. Boxing happens in a ring, a square with ropes. Both shapes have long histories, and both were once linked to trouble with the law.

Capoeira grew among Africans and their children in Brazil. A law of 1890 made it a crime. Teachers in Salvador later opened schools, and in 2014 UNESCO honored the capoeira circle. Boxing in England moved from bare-knuckle prize fights to the gloved Queensberry Rules of 1867.

In this unit, you will read old pictures, laws and rule books. You will explain how capoeira moved from the street to the academy. You will compare who runs boxing in schools, colleges, clubs and town gyms.
bigQuestion: How can an art that the law once pushed out become a sport with schools, rule books and honors?

choices: in Brazil, among Africans and their children
test.why: Capoeira is Afro-Brazilian; it grew among Africans and their children in Brazil.

test.q: What did Article 402 of Brazil's 1890 Penal Code do?
choices: made capoeira in streets and squares a crime
test.why: Article 402 made capoeira in streets and public squares a crime.

test.q: Who opened a capoeira academy in Salvador in 1932?
test.why: Mestre Bimba opened his academy in 1932; it became the home of Capoeira Regional.

test.q: Which style did Mestre Pastinha work to keep?
test.why: Pastinha's center, opened in 1941, kept Capoeira Angola, the older style.
In 2014 UNESCO added the capoeira circle to its intangible heritage list.
Chambers wrote them; the Marquess backed them and lent his name.

test.q: What was new about the Queensberry Rules?
choices: bare fists and no time limit
gloves, three-minute rounds and a ten-second count
a round ended when a boxer fell
test.why: Queensberry set gloves, three-minute rounds with rest, and a ten-second count.

test.q: Which fight was held with gloves under Queensberry Rules?
test.why: Corbett beat Sullivan with gloves under Queensberry Rules in New Orleans in 1892.

test.q: Why is the Rugendas picture useful but limited?
choices: it is a record from the time, but made by an outsider
it was written by the police
test.why: The picture is a primary source from the 1820s, but a visiting painter made it.

test.q: Why did Brazil's 1888 law leave many freed people poor?
choices: it gave no land, money or schooling
test.why: The Golden Law ended slavery but gave freed people nothing else.

choices: a bare-knuckle match fought for money
test.why: Prize fights in the 1700s and 1800s were bare-knuckle matches fought for money.

test.q: Who ran the first Golden Gloves tournaments?
choices: newspapers in New York and Chicago
test.why: The New York Daily News began them in 1927; the Chicago Tribune followed in 1928.

test.q: Why did the NCAA stop its boxing championships?
choices: a Wisconsin boxer, Charlie Mohr, died after the 1960 tournament
test.why: After Charlie Mohr's death in 1960, the NCAA ended its boxing championships.

test.q: How do capoeira and boxing histories look alike?
choices: both were once pushed by law out of public places, then moved into schools and rule books
test.why: Capoeira was banned in 1890; prize fights were illegal in many places. Both later gained schools, rules and governing bodies.

test.q: Which of these is a governing body?
test.why: The Amateur Boxing Association, founded in 1880, wrote rules and ran championships.

write.prompt: Did laws help or hurt capoeira and boxing? Choose one side or a mix. Use at least two records from this unit, such as Article 402 of Brazil's 1890 Penal Code, the Golden Law of 1888, Bimba's 1937 license, the UNESCO listing of 2014, the Queensberry Rules of 1867 or the 1889 Sullivan and Kilrain fight. Name each record and its year, say what it did, and explain how people responded.
